title: The investor with 66% annual returns ended up 4× poorer than the one with 22%. Housel's point about time, with an Indian example.
author: iktisab
selftext:
From Morgan Housel, The Psychology of Money (2020):



\- Jim Simons compounded at 66% a year since 1988. Net worth at the time of writing: $21B.

\- Warren Buffett compounded at roughly 22%. Net worth: $84.5B.

\- Buffett started serious investing at 10; Simons found his stride at 50.

\- $81.5B of Buffett's $84.5B came after his mid-60s (about 96%).

\- Housel's thought experiment: had Buffett started at 30 with $25,000 and stopped at 60, same 22%, he'd have about $11.9M.



Indian illustration (my calculation, assumes 12% a year, before tax and inflation):

₹5,000/month from 25 to 60 → ₹2.76 crore (₹21 lakh invested)

₹5,000/month from 35 to 60 → ₹85 lakh (₹15 lakh invested)



Ten years of delay costs about ₹1.9 crore. Not a forecast, just the arithmetic of compounding.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the Simons line always bugs me. 66% was Medallion's return, and his money came mostly from owning the firm and its fees, not from compounding his own pot at 66%. the point about time holds, that example just doesn't show it.

replies.author: iktisab
replies.body: Its tested data... It doesnt show the exact source. Its just shows compounding.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: right, a compounding table is just arithmetic. it'll turn 66% into any number you like. the years it doesn't happen are the part nobody tabulates.
